Critics say Anthropic’s IPO could test its safety commitment : NPR

Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Critics say Anthropic’s IPO could test its safety commitment Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
Technology
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
November 21, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Katie McQue
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, is seen on video outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square as shares begin trading after the company's IPO on Nov. 19, 2026. Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety first will be tested.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
hide caption
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
Technology
Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
Understanding AI
California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.
The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.
That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.
"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.
The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.
Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.
"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.
The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.
"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.
In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so

hide caption
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
Understanding AI
Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs call for AI development to slow down, OpenAI to delay IPO
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
What happened with stock markets this week?
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
What's behind the steep drops?
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Technology
U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025.
Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images
What are the potential financial consequences?
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness.
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
What does it mean for the economy if the AI boom falters?
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.

articles.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
articles.text:
S&P 500 sinks and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
S&P 500 sinks and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
Business
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
November 20, 20265:11 PM ET
By
The Associated Press
Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.
Seth Wenig/AP
hide caption
Seth Wenig/AP
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
Technology
Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Pirates, privateers, and the future of those seized Iran-linked oil tankers : Planet Money The U.S. is working on bringing back the ancient maritime practice of prize law — which allowed for privateers, or more recently, navies, to seize enemy-linked ships, and quickly sell them off.
Why? Well, the U.S. has been seizing lots of big boats — oil tankers linked to Iran and Venezuela — in what the Pentagon calls an effort to disrupt ‘illicit networks.’ But after they seize the big boats, they have a big problem: Boats are very expensive to maintain, and each day the government owns them adds extra costs. So they want to sell off the tankers and the oil inside as soon as possible.
On today’s show, pirates, some swashbuckling, and an interview with the federal judge tasked with standing up a modern-day prize court.

articles.text:
Old software, what games make money, and long TV shows : Planet Money : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Old software, what games make money, and long TV shows : Planet Money In a week of outages, we're thinking about the rising threat of AI-powered cyberattacks. But sometimes, it's not the most sophisticated attack that's concerning, but the easy targets buried in old software.
NPR
Planet Money

Planet Money
Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
November 20, 20267:00 AM ET
Cooper Katz McKim
You're reading a newsletter from  The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter.  Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
There is a certain thrill in spotting a dollar bill on the ground. It's free money! Well one lucky person found a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her aunt's closet, under a pile of fur coats. The Smithsonian magazine reported the painting, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I," is part of a three-part series based on Keeffe's time in northern New Mexico. O'Keeffe has described her time there as particularly impactful.
Georgia O'Keeffe's "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I" (Screenshot captured on Christie's  auction page)
hide caption
The woman's aunt received the painting as a graduation gift from her parents way back when. They bought it for $3,800. That's the equivalent of $42,000 in today's dollars. This week, it sold at Christie's for $4,878,000 million. Double check your closet, people.
Coming up:
Why old software is so risky
Why Steam is pulling in less revenue from NEW games
What cohost Adrian Ma is reading this week
News We're Watching
This has been a long and strange week of outages from United Airlines to Apple Pay to the F.A.A. It's got many people thinking about this seemingly omnipresent threat of cyberattack. The agencies and companies experiencing the outages insist they're unrelated to cyberattacks. But there is a lot of concern right now about how vulnerable the U.S. is to these digital threats with the combination of fast-growing AI and decidedly fragile infrastructure.
Case in point, earlier this month, Europe faced ANOTHER hack on its supermarket refrigeration. Grocery stores and butcher shops across seven countries saw their fridges and freezers turned up to more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
It wasn't some complicated, sophisticated attack. It was hackers that found a vulnerability in old software. A vulnerability that had existed for a long time.
"That's where attackers see a big opportunity," said Aaron Mitchell, CEO of HeroDevs. "That's an easy way for me to get access and start to do some real damage."
After all, there is a lot of old software out there. Ones that touch utilities, hospitals, and critical infrastructure - or airlines. In some cases, companies didn't feel much urgency to address security gaps.
Employees empty freezers after a hacker attack raised the temperature in the freezers to 50 degrees Celsius (Photo by Johan NILSSON / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images) / Sweden OUT
JOHAN NILSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
hide caption
JOHAN NILSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
HeroDevs is a cybersecurity firm that does the addressing FOR companies. They help maintain support for a certain kind of software called open-source. When a software reaches end-of-life, and a company has moved on to new ideas, they might pay HeroDevs to maintain it and (importantly!!) patch vulnerabilities.
That could be more important than ever because AI is helping find a record number of these vulnerabilities. Last week, VulnCheck, a cybersecurity consulting firm, posted that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been found and disclosed so far this year, more than double than 2025. Hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities 33% faster compared to 2025.
In other words, vulnerabilities in outdated software are a prime target for hackers.
"About half of all exploits that happen, known exploits of a vulnerability, are happening on versions that are no longer supported by the maintainer," said Mitchell. "That number is rapidly growing."
This is a problem because countless websites, companies, and governments have outdated software somewhere.
Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that's built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.
"It was a huge deal, and for the whole week the whole internet was kind of on fire trying to get this thing patched," said Mitchell.
Still, in some cases, Mitchell said there were documented cases of websites that DID get exploited.
This is one example of how a small entrance for bad guys can be so dangerous. But these little doorways keep popping up. On Tuesday, an AI company revealed a critical vulnerability in Java known as Java4Shell prompting websites and companies to quickly take actions to patch against it.
As we can see and perhaps even feel, hackers are taking advantage. The most common cyberattack on utilities involves outdated software. Early this month, a cyberattack hit French blood banks, looking to increase temperatures using a similar tactic to the refrigeration hacks, although French authorities caught the attack in time and stopped it.
Richard Horne, the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said that "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long." In 2028, the UK predicts AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
For now, Aaron Mitchell says, exploitation of vulnerabilities isn't taking off as much as it could be, "but every day that goes by, we get that much closer to the edge."

articles.text:
This is how Trump got so rich with crypto : NPR

This is how Trump got so rich with crypto President Trump has made billions of dollars in his second term — most of it in cryptocurrencies. Democrats are vowing to probe his businesses as they gear up to take over Congress next year.
Business
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
November 20, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Rafael Nam
Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates
Listen
3:48
3:48
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6038969/nx-s1-9998322" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
President Trump tossing a coin before the Army v. Navy football game in Philadelphia on Dec. 14, 2019.
Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.
Elections
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Trump's meme coin
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Elections
The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.
A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, is set to become chair of the House Oversight Committee in January.
Mark Schiefelbein/AP
hide caption
Mark Schiefelbein/AP
A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm
But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.
Diplomacy
Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.
Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.
The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.
Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build b
